```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
library(modelr)

set.seed(1)

dir.create("plots", showWarnings = FALSE)
```


## Problem 1

Import and clean the WP homicide data.

```{r}
homicide_df =
  read_csv("data/homicide-data.csv", na = c("", "NA", "Unknown")) |>
  mutate(
    city_state = str_c(city, ", ", state),
    resolved = as.numeric(disposition == "Closed by arrest"),
    victim_age = as.numeric(victim_age)
  ) |>
  filter(
    !(city_state %in% c("Dallas, TX", "Phoenix, AZ", "Kansas City, MO", "Tulsa, AL")),
    victim_race %in% c("White", "Black")
  ) |>
  mutate(victim_race = fct_relevel(victim_race, "White")) |>
  select(city_state, resolved, victim_age, victim_race, victim_sex)
```

The cleaned dataset has `r nrow(homicide_df)` homicides in `r n_distinct(pull(homicide_df, city_state))` cities. Key variables are `city_state`, `resolved` (1 = closed by arrest), `victim_age`, `victim_race` (White / Black) and `victim_sex`.

Fit the logistic regression for Baltimore.

```{r}
baltimore_fit =
  homicide_df |>
  filter(city_state == "Baltimore, MD") |>
  glm(resolved ~ victim_age + victim_sex + victim_race, data = _, family = binomial())

baltimore_or =
  baltimore_fit |>
  broom::tidy() |>
  filter(term == "victim_sexMale") |>
  mutate(
    OR = exp(estimate),
    ci_lower = exp(estimate - 1.96 * std.error),
    ci_upper = exp(estimate + 1.96 * std.error)
  ) |>
  select(term, OR, ci_lower, ci_upper, p.value)

baltimore_or |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

**Sex and solving homicides in Baltimore:**

OR = `r round(pull(baltimore_or, OR), 3)`, 95% CI: (`r round(pull(baltimore_or, ci_lower), 3)`, `r round(pull(baltimore_or, ci_upper), 3)`), p < 0.001.

Therefore, keeping age and race fixed, homicides with male victims have lower odds of being solved than those with female victims.

Now fit the model for each city.

```{r}
city_or_df =
  homicide_df |>
  nest(data = -city_state) |>
  mutate(
    fits = map(data, \(df) glm(resolved ~ victim_age + victim_sex + victim_race, data = df, family = binomial())),
    results = map(fits, broom::tidy)
  ) |>
  select(city_state, results) |>
  unnest(results) |>
  filter(term == "victim_sexMale") |>
  mutate(
    OR = exp(estimate),
    ci_lower = exp(estimate - 1.96 * std.error),
    ci_upper = exp(estimate + 1.96 * std.error)
  ) |>
  select(city_state, OR, ci_lower, ci_upper)

city_or_df |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

Plot the ORs and CIs.

```{r, fig.asp = 1.2}
city_or_plot =
  city_or_df |>
  mutate(city_state = fct_reorder(city_state, OR)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = city_state, y = OR)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = ci_lower, ymax = ci_upper)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Adjusted OR for solving homicides (male vs female victims)",
    x = "City",
    y = "Odds ratio (95% CI)"
  )

city_or_plot

ggsave("plots/city_or_plot.png", city_or_plot, width = 8, height = 10)
```

Most cities have OR below 1, so homicides with male victims are generally less likely to be solved than those with female victims. New York has the lowest OR (0.262), while Albuquerque has the highest (1.767). Many CIs cross 1, and cities with high ORs (e.g. Albuquerque, Stockton, Fresno) have wide CIs, likely due to small samples.

## Problem 2

Load the Central Park weather data.

```{r}
data("weather_df")

weather_df =
  weather_df |>
  filter(name == "CentralPark_NY") |>
  drop_na(tmax, tmin, prcp)
```

The data have `r nrow(weather_df)` daily observations from Central Park, including `date`, `prcp`, `tmax` and `tmin`.

Draw 5000 bootstrap samples, fit the model, and get r^2 and the product of the two slopes.

```{r}
boot_df =
  weather_df |>
  modelr::bootstrap(n = 5000) |>
  mutate(
    fits = map(strap, \(df) lm(tmax ~ tmin + prcp, data = df)),
    glance_res = map(fits, broom::glance),
    tidy_res = map(fits, broom::tidy),
    r_squared = map_dbl(glance_res, \(df) pull(df, r.squared)),
    beta_product = map_dbl(
      tidy_res,
      \(df) df |> filter(term != "(Intercept)") |> pull(estimate) |> prod()
    )
  ) |>
  select(.id, r_squared, beta_product)
```

Plot the distributions.

```{r}
boot_plot =
  boot_df |>
  pivot_longer(
    r_squared:beta_product,
    names_to = "quantity",
    values_to = "estimate"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = estimate)) +
  geom_density() +
  facet_wrap(~quantity, scales = "free") +
  labs(
    title = "Bootstrap distributions (5000 samples)",
    x = "Estimate",
    y = "Density"
  )

boot_plot

ggsave("plots/boot_plot.png", boot_plot, width = 8, height = 5)
```

The distribution of r^2 is unimodal and slightly left-skewed, peaking around 0.915, so tmin and prcp explain most of the variation in tmax. The distribution of the slope product is also unimodal, peaking around -0.002 with a slight right tail, because the prcp slope is very small and close to 0.

95% CIs from the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles:

```{r}
boot_df |>
  pivot_longer(
    r_squared:beta_product,
    names_to = "quantity",
    values_to = "estimate"
  ) |>
  group_by(quantity) |>
  summarize(
    ci_lower = quantile(estimate, 0.025),
    ci_upper = quantile(estimate, 0.975)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 4)
```

The 95% CI for r^2 is (0.894, 0.928), and the 95% CI for the slope product is (-0.0051, 0.0012). Therefore, the model fits the data well, and the product of the two slopes is not clearly different from 0, since its CI includes 0.
